questions.context: You are telling a friend about a special meal your grandmother cooked last Sunday.
questions.instruction:
Complete the sentence with the correct article (a, an, the) or write 'no article' if none is needed:

My grandmother made ___ delicious lamb stew, and everyone at the table asked for seconds.
questions.hint: Think about whether this is the first time the lamb stew is being mentioned.
questions.explanation: Use 'a' the first time you introduce something — here, the lamb stew is being mentioned for the first time, so it's 'a delicious lamb stew'.

commonWrongAnswers.comment: 'The' works when both you and your listener already know which specific stew you mean — but this is the first time you're mentioning it, so 'a' is the right choice here.
'An' goes before words that start with a vowel sound — 'delicious' starts with a 'd' sound, so you need 'a', not 'an'.
Skipping the article entirely sounds unnatural with a singular countable noun like 'stew' when you're introducing it for the first time.

questions.context: You are writing in your diary about a conversation with your father last week. He told you he was confident about something.
questions.instruction:
Complete the sentence with the correct modal past form:

My father said he ___ always be there for us, no matter what happened.
questions.hint: The original words were 'I will always be there for you' — now you are reporting them in the past.
questions.explanation: When you report someone's words in the past, 'will' shifts back to 'would' — that's the standard backshift rule in reported speech.

commonWrongAnswers.comment: 'Will' is what your father actually said at the time, but because you're reporting it in the past tense ('said'), you need to shift it back to 'would'.
'Could' is the past form of 'can', not 'will' — it changes the meaning to ability rather than the promise your father was making.
'Should' adds a sense of obligation or advice, which changes your father's meaning — he was making a promise, not giving instructions.

questions.context: A teenager wrote this sentence in an essay about family responsibilities.
questions.instruction:
The sentence below contains one grammar error. Rewrite the entire sentence correctly:

My parents always insisted on me to do the washing-up after dinner.
questions.correctAnswer: My parents always insisted on me doing the washing-up after dinner.
questions.explanation: After 'insist on', the next verb must be a gerund (-ing form), not an infinitive — so it's 'insisted on me doing', not 'to do'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: My parents always insisted on me to doing the washing-up after dinner.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: You've added -ing but kept 'to' as well — you only need one or the other, and after 'insist on' the correct choice is 'doing' without 'to'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: My parents always insisted me to do the washing-up after dinner.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: Removing 'on' loses the fixed phrase 'insist on' — and the verb after it still needs to be 'doing', not 'to do'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: My parents always insisted on me to do the washing up after dinner.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: The hyphen in 'washing-up' is a minor point, but the main issue remains: after 'insist on' you need a gerund, so 'doing' is required instead of 'to do'.

questions.context: You are reading a message your aunt sent after learning that your cousin missed an important family reunion.
questions.instruction:
The sentence below contains one grammar error. Rewrite the entire sentence correctly:

He must have told us he wasn't coming so we could have made other arrangements.
questions.correctAnswer: He should have told us he wasn't coming so we could have made other arrangements.
questions.explanation: 'Should have' expresses that something was the right thing to do but wasn't done — 'must have' means you're almost certain something happened, which doesn't fit here.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: He must have tell us he wasn't coming so we could have made other arrangements.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: You've kept 'must have' and also changed 'told' to 'tell', but 'must have' is still the wrong modal here — and after 'have' you always need a past participle like 'told', not the base form 'tell'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: He should have tell us he wasn't coming so we could have made other arrangements.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: You've chosen the right modal 'should have', but the verb after 'have' must be a past participle — so it's 'told', not 'tell'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: He should told us he wasn't coming so we could have made other arrangements.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: 'Should' on its own needs 'have' between it and the past participle to talk about a missed past action — the full form is 'should have told'.

questions.context: You are describing what was happening at home when your elder brother suddenly arrived for a surprise visit.
questions.instruction:
Complete the sentence with the correct form of the verb in brackets:

When my brother rang the doorbell, my mother ___ (prepare) dinner in the kitchen.
questions.hint: Think about which tense shows an action that was already in progress at a specific moment in the past.
questions.explanation: The past continuous ('was preparing') shows that the action was already in progress at the exact moment something else happened — perfect for describing what mum was doing when the doorbell rang.

commonWrongAnswers.comment: Simple past describes a completed action, but here dinner-making was still in progress when the doorbell rang — that's a job for the past continuous 'was preparing'.
The present perfect continuous connects the past to now, but this sentence is set entirely in the past with a clear past moment ('rang'), so 'was preparing' is the right tense.
Past perfect suggests the preparation was fully finished before the doorbell rang — but the sentence implies she was still in the middle of cooking, so 'was preparing' fits better.
